Before you tint

Tinted paint usually can't come back, so a quick check saves a mis-tint.

Reading a tint label

Each column is one colorant. The Oz row is whole ounces and the 384th row is 384ths of an ounce, so "EL 0 | 29" means 29/384 oz of Pthalo Blue (about 2.2 mL). Formulas depend on the product, base and can size, so only the tint machine can make one. A formula from one base won't match in another.

  • AXL Permanent Yellow
  • BL Lamp Black
  • CL Yellow Oxide
  • DL Pthalo Green
  • EL Pthalo Blue
  • FL Red Oxide
  • IL Brown Oxide
  • JL Violet
  • KXL White
  • LL Raw Umber
  • RL Exterior Red
  • RUL High Hide Red
  • TL Medium Yellow
  • VL Magenta
  • VUL High Hide Violet
  • YL High Hide Yellow

Swatches are rough guides to each colorant, not exact.

Limewash: how it works and how to do it

What limewash is

Slaked lime, water and mineral pigment. On bare masonry it soaks in and cures back into limestone, so it isn't a film like paint: it breathes, it's dead flat and chalky, and every wall comes out cloudy and a little different. It goes on dark and dries much lighter. For painted drywall there are mineral washes that give the same look. Neither one likes being scrubbed.

Where it works
  • True limewash: bare brick, stone, stucco and unpainted masonry, inside or out. Soak the surface first. No primer.
  • Painted drywall: use a mineral wash made for walls, like Romabio Velatura. True limewash can chalk or ghost on drywall. Add a mineral primer if the old paint is glossy or uneven.
  • Skip it: high-traffic walls and anything that gets scrubbed, like kids' rooms or behind the stove.
What goes in the basket
  • Brick or masonry: a true limewash, like Romabio Classico
  • Painted drywall: a mineral wash, like Romabio Velatura, plus mineral primer if the wall is uneven
  • 4–6" natural bristle block brush. No roller for the wash itself.
  • Bucket, stir stick or paddle mixer, and a jug to measure the water
  • Pump sprayer to soak brick first
  • Drop cloths, painter's tape, gloves and safety glasses: lime is caustic
Colors that work

Limewash wants mineral colors: warm whites, greige and stone greys, clay and terracotta, sand and ochre, sage, dusty blue, charcoal. Bright, saturated colors go muddy, and the lime lightens everything. Romabio's own shelf colors (Avorio White, Bianco White, Nube Gray, Riposo Beige) are the safe picks. These catalog colors have the same character: tap one to put it on the walls.

Sheens: see what the shine really does

One long wall, one color, all six sheens side by side under the same light. Drag on the wall to move the light. Each panel has a patch, a taped seam and roller marks, so you can see what each sheen shows and hides.

Paint color
Why more shine shows more

Every paint reflects about the same small amount of light. Flat paint's surface is rough, so that light scatters every direction and you just see color. Glossy paint is smooth, so the light bounces back in one direction: bright highlights, window reflections, and every bump, patch and roller mark. It's strongest when you look along the wall, so that's where the difference jumps out.

Wood colors in paint

Colores de madera. Find the paint that looks like caoba, nogal, roble and more. Tap any chip to see it on your walls.

Wood looks are typical of the finished wood, and real boards vary. Colors on screen are close but not exact, so check a paint sample.

Wood
Stain color · Varathane Premium
Topcoat

Stain only adds color. The topcoat is what protects the wood and sets the shine.

See it in the room
What are you staining?
How stain works

Stain is color suspended in a liquid. It soaks into the wood's pores, then you wipe away whatever stays on top. Porous wood takes more, so the grain shows through. That's why the same can looks different on oak and pine, and why the sample always goes on your actual wood.

Stain gives color, not protection. Wipe off every bit of the extra, let it dry, and seal it with a topcoat. Stain left sitting on top never dries properly and the finish won't stick to it.

Which product does what
When it goes wrong
Blotchy patches

Soft wood soaked up stain unevenly. Next time use wood conditioner, or gel stain, which sits closer to the surface. To fix it, sand back and start over; a darker stain can hide mild blotching.

Too dark

Wipe it down right away with a rag dampened with mineral spirits (oil stain) or water (water-based stain). Next time wipe sooner. Once dry, the only way back is sanding.

Too light

Let it sit longer before wiping. With Classic or gel stain, add another coat after it dries. Premium Fast Dry is made for one coat, so test a darker color instead.

Still sticky hours later

Too much was left on the surface. Wipe it with a rag dampened with mineral spirits, let it dry fully, and then topcoat. Cool or damp weather also slows drying.

Bubbles in the poly

The can was shaken, or the coat was over-brushed. Stir gently and lay it on in long, light strokes. Once dry, sand the bubbles flat and recoat.

Lap marks and streaks

The edge dried before the next pass. Work smaller sections, keep a wet edge, and finish with the grain from end to end.

Safety
  • Oily rags can catch fire by themselves. Never leave them balled up or in the trash. Put them in a sealed, water-filled metal container until you can dispose of them properly.
  • Sanding old paint or finish can release lead dust. In older homes, test first.
  • Keep windows open and follow the can. Dry times assume about 70°F and 50% humidity, and go longer when it's cool or damp.

Based on Varathane product sheets. Formulas and times change, so the directions on the can win. Stain chips are screen approximations: always test on your own wood.
